title: Resource Monitoring
lead: Read CPU, load, memory and disk with uptime, free, df, top and friends, and find out what is slowing the system down.
objectives: You read the load average relative to the number of CPU cores (nproc).
You tell free memory from available memory and understand buff/cache.
You check disk usage with df and du and find big folders.
You find the top CPU and memory consumers with top, htop and ps.

sections.title: Load and CPU: uptime, nproc, lscpu
body: When a server feels slow, look at the **load average** first. `uptime` shows three numbers: the average load of the last **1, 5 and 15 minutes**. The same values live in `/proc/loadavg`.

A load number alone means nothing. Read it **relative to the number of cores** (`nproc`). On a 4-core machine a load of 4.0 means fully used, 8.0 means processes are waiting in line (saturation). Rule of thumb: load below the core count is fine, load above it means overload.
Compare the three values: 1 min higher than 15 min means the load is rising now; 1 min lower than 15 min means it is calming down.

commands.what: Shows the time, how long the system has been up, logged-in users and the load average (1, 5, 15 min).
commands.where: As the very first look at a slow server.
commands.why: One line tells you if the machine is busy and in which direction it is going.

commands.what: Prints the number of available CPU cores (threads).
commands.where: Together with uptime to judge the load.
commands.why: Load 4.0 is fine on 8 cores but saturated on 2 cores.

commands.what: Shows CPU details: model, sockets, cores, threads, MHz.
commands.where: When you need to know what hardware the VM or server really has.
commands.why: Confirms how many cores you have and whether they are virtual.

commands.what: Raw load data: three load values, running/total tasks and the last PID.
commands.where: In scripts, or when uptime is not installed.
commands.why: It is the source that uptime and top read from.

sections.tip: Quick check: if the first load value divided by `nproc` is above 1, the CPU is saturated.

sections.title: Memory: free, /proc/meminfo, vmstat
body: `free -h` shows RAM and swap in readable units. Do not panic about a small **free** value: Linux uses unused RAM as cache (**buff/cache**) and gives it back when programs need it.

The column that matters is **available**: it estimates how much memory new programs can get without swapping. Low *available* plus heavy swap use means real memory shortage. Details are in `/proc/meminfo` (`MemTotal`, `MemFree`, `MemAvailable`).
`vmstat` shows memory, swap, I/O and CPU in one table. Columns `si`/`so` (swap in/out) above zero for a long time and a high `wa` (waiting for I/O) are warning signs.

commands.what: Shows total, used, free, shared, buff/cache and available RAM and swap in human-readable units.
commands.where: When the system is slow and you suspect full RAM.
commands.why: Looking at available instead of free prevents false alarms.

commands.what: Prints the detailed kernel memory statistics.
commands.where: For scripts or when you need exact values like MemAvailable or SwapFree.
commands.why: It is the source behind free.

commands.what: Prints a CPU, memory, swap and I/O line every second, five times.
commands.where: To see trends over a few seconds instead of one snapshot.
commands.why: Shows swapping (si/so) and I/O wait (wa) that top hides at first glance.

sections.tip: Ignore the first line of `vmstat`; it shows averages since boot. The following lines are live.

sections.title: Disk: df, du, iostat
body: A full disk causes strange errors: services crash, logs cannot be written. `df -h` shows usage per filesystem, `du` shows which folder uses the space.
Workflow: `df -h` finds the full filesystem, then `du -sh /var/*` or `du -h /var | sort -h | tail` finds the big folders. `sort -h` understands sizes like 4K, 12M, 3G.
`iostat` comes from the **sysstat** package and shows disk activity. High `%util` and `await` mean the disk is the bottleneck.

commands.what: Shows size, used, available and percentage per mounted filesystem.
commands.where: As the first check for 'No space left on device'.
commands.why: You see which mount point is nearly full (Use%).

commands.what: Shows the total size of a folder (-s summary, -h readable).
commands.where: To measure a single folder such as your home or /var/log.
commands.why: Answers 'how big is this?' with one line.

commands.what: Lists sizes of all subfolders, sorted from small to large.
commands.where: To find the biggest folders; add `| tail -n 5` for the top five.

commands.what: Extended disk statistics every second, three times (needs the sysstat package).
commands.where: When the system is slow but CPU and RAM look fine.
commands.why: Shows whether the disk is saturated (%util, await).

sections.tip: Install sysstat: Ubuntu/Debian `sudo apt install sysstat`, Rocky/Alma `sudo dnf install sysstat`.
sections.warn: `du` on `/` can run for minutes and load the disk. Limit it to one folder, for example `du -h /var | sort -h | tail`.

sections.title: Processes: top, htop, ps
body: `top` is the live task manager of the terminal. The header shows load, tasks, CPU and memory; below is the process list. In `top`: `P` sorts by CPU, `M` by memory, `q` quits.

`htop` is the colourful, easier version. It is not installed by default. Ubuntu/Debian: `sudo apt install htop`. On Rocky/Alma it lives in the **EPEL** repository: first `sudo dnf install epel-release`, then `sudo dnf install htop`.

For scripts and logs use batch mode: `top -b -n 1` prints one snapshot and exits. `ps aux --sort=-%mem | head` lists the top memory consumers, `--sort=-%cpu` the top CPU consumers (the minus means descending).

commands.what: Live view of load, CPU, memory and processes; refreshes every 3 seconds.
commands.where: To see right now who is using resources.
commands.why: Finds the PID of the problem process.

commands.what: Batch mode: prints one snapshot and exits.
commands.where: In scripts, tickets and when piping to head or grep.
commands.why: You can save or filter the output, for example `top -b -n 1 | head -n 15`.

commands.what: Interactive process viewer with colours, bars and mouse support.
commands.where: Daily work on servers and VMs.
commands.why: Easier to read and to sort than top.

commands.what: Lists processes sorted by memory use, highest first, first 10 lines.
commands.where: When RAM is nearly full and you look for the culprit.
commands.why: Shows user, PID, %CPU, %MEM and command in a copyable list.

commands.what: Lists processes sorted by CPU use, highest first.
commands.why: Finds the CPU hog without an interactive screen.

sections.tip: In `top` press `1` to see every core separately and `c` to see full command lines.

sections.title: Triage: a fixed order
body: When a ticket says 'the server is slow', follow the same order each time: **1.** `uptime` and `nproc` (load vs cores), **2.** `free -h` (available memory, swap), **3.** `df -h` (full disk), **4.** `top` or `ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head` (who is the culprit), **5.** `vmstat 1 5` / `iostat -x` (swap or disk bottleneck).
Decide: high load and high `us` CPU means a CPU problem. High load with low CPU but high `wa` means disk or network I/O. Low available memory and swap activity means a RAM problem.
To practise on your VM you need load. Use a time limit: `timeout 30 yes > /dev/null &` starts one CPU hog that stops after 30 seconds. See the VM section.
sections.tip: Write down the numbers before you change anything. A ticket answer like 'load 4.5 on 2 cores, python3 uses 85% CPU' is worth more than 'it is slow'.
sections.warn: Load generators such as `yes > /dev/null &` or `stress-ng` run until stopped. Always use `timeout` and clean up with `pkill yes` afterwards.
sections.danger: Never start a load generator or kill processes on a production server. Practise only on your own VM, and take a snapshot first.

t01.text: Show uptime and the load average with `uptime`.
t01.hint: Three numbers after 'load average:' are 1, 5 and 15 minutes.

t02.text: Show memory in readable units with `free -h`. Find the `available` column.

t03.text: Show the disk usage of all filesystems with `df -h`.

t04.text: Find where the `free` program lives with `which free`.

t05.text: The file `~/lab/loadavg.txt` is a copy of `/proc/loadavg`. Show it with `cat ~/lab/loadavg.txt`.
t05.hint: The first three numbers are the 1, 5 and 15 minute load.

t06.text: The machine has the number of cores in `~/lab/cores.txt`. Read it with `cat ~/lab/cores.txt`, compare it with the 1-minute load 4.52, and write your verdict (`overloaded` or `ok`) into `~/lab/load_verdict.txt` with `echo`.
t06.hint: Load 4.52 on 2 cores is above the core count: `echo overloaded > ~/lab/load_verdict.txt`.

t07.text: In `~/lab/meminfo.txt` find the line `MemAvailable` with `grep MemAvailable ~/lab/meminfo.txt`.
t07.hint: MemAvailable is the number that matters, not MemFree.

t08.text: In `~/lab/top_snapshot.txt` show the CPU line with `grep Cpu ~/lab/top_snapshot.txt`.
t08.hint: `us` is user time, `wa` is I/O wait, `id` is idle.

t09.text: Predict: which value will `free -h | grep Mem` show in the `available` column? Think first, then run it.
t09.hint: Look at the last column of the Mem line.

t10.text: Predict: how many lines does `grep -c java ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt` print? Think first, then run it.

t11.text: Predict: what does `cut -d ' ' -f 1 ~/lab/loadavg.txt` print? Think first, then run it.
t11.hint: -d sets the separator, -f 1 is the first field.

t12.text: Find the top CPU consumers in the snapshot: `sort -k3 -nr ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt | head -n 3`. Which process is first?

t13.text: Mini: save the top 2 memory consumers of `~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt` into `~/lab/top_mem.txt`. Sort by column 4 with `sort -k4 -nr`, take two lines with `head -n 2` and redirect with `>`.

t14.text: Debug: `~/lab/monitor_cmds.txt` lists the wrong commands (`nprocs` does not exist and `free -m` is not human-readable). Rewrite the file with `printf` so it contains `cores: nproc`, `memory: free -h` and `disk: df -h`, one per line.

t15.text: Mini: `~/lab/du_report.txt` has sizes in KB. Save the 3 biggest entries into `~/lab/biggest.txt` with `sort -nr`, `head -n 3` and `>`.

t16.text: Challenge: build `~/lab/report.txt` with three parts: the 1-minute load from `~/lab/loadavg.txt` (use `cut`), the `MemAvailable` line from `~/lab/meminfo.txt` (use `grep`, append with `>>`) and your verdict `overloaded` (use `echo`, append).
t16.hint: The first command uses `>`, the others `>>`, so nothing is overwritten.

t17.text: TICKET #5201 — The server linux-lab is very slow. In `~/lab/top_snapshot.txt` is the output of `top -b -n 1`. Find the process with the highest CPU use and write its name and its user into `~/lab/culprit.txt`.
t17.hint: Look at the first process line with `head -n 9 ~/lab/top_snapshot.txt`, then `echo "name user" > ~/lab/culprit.txt`.

q1.q: Which memory value tells you how much RAM new programs can really get?
q1.explain: free is only unused RAM. Linux also uses RAM as cache; available includes the part it can give back, so it is the right value.

q2.q: A 4-core machine shows a 1-minute load of 8.0. What does that mean?
options: The CPU is saturated: processes wait in line
q2.explain: Load is read relative to the cores. Load 8 on 4 cores means twice as many runnable tasks as cores.

q3.q: How do you install htop on Rocky Linux?
options: sudo dnf install htop directly, always works
sudo dnf install epel-release, then sudo dnf install htop
q3.explain: On the RHEL family htop is in the EPEL repository, so enable EPEL first. apt is for Debian/Ubuntu.

q4.q: Which command lists the top memory consumers?
q4.explain: ps with --sort=-%mem sorts by memory descending; head shows the first lines.

summary: Read the load average (1/5/15 min) relative to `nproc`; load above the core count means saturation.
`free -h`: look at available, not free; buff/cache is reusable.
`df -h` finds the full filesystem, `du -sh` and `du -h | sort -h` the big folders.
`top`, `htop` (EPEL on Rocky/Alma), `top -b -n 1` and `ps aux --sort=-%mem | head` find the culprit.
`vmstat` and `iostat` (sysstat) reveal swap and disk bottlenecks.
Test load only on your own VM, with `timeout`, after a snapshot.

glossary.meaning: Average number of tasks running or waiting for CPU/I-O over 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
Load is higher than the core count; work waits in a queue.
RAM used for file caches; the kernel frees it when needed.
Estimate of memory that new programs can use without swapping.
Disk space used as an emergency extension of RAM; slow.
Extra Packages for Enterprise Linux: additional repository for RHEL, Rocky and Alma.
Share of time the CPU waits for disk or network.

vm.intro: Run these on your own VM (Ubuntu, Rocky, Alma or WSL). Monitoring commands are harmless; only the last task creates load. Take a snapshot before it.

v01.title: Load and cores
v01.text: Show the load average and the number of cores. Is the 1-minute load below the core count? Paste the output of `uptime`.
differs: The numbers will be different; only the format matters.
On WSL `uptime` may show a very short uptime. That is normal.

v02.title: Memory: free vs available
v02.text: Look at memory. Compare the free and available columns. Paste the output.

blocks.expected:
total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:          3.8Gi       612Mi       2.4Gi        12Mi       860Mi       3.0Gi
Swap:         2.0Gi          0B       2.0Gi
MemTotal:        3980000 kB
MemFree:         2500000 kB
MemAvailable:    3100000 kB

differs: Without swap the Swap line shows 0B; that is fine.
On older systems the `available` column may be missing; use MemAvailable from /proc/meminfo.

v03.title: Disk usage
v03.text: Find the filesystem usage and the five biggest folders under `/var`. Paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
df -h
du -sh ~
sudo du -h /var 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -n 5
blocks.expected:
Filesystem           Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/rhel-root  20G  4.1G   16G  21% /
...

differs: On WSL you see extra mounts like /mnt/c; ignore them.

v04.title: vmstat, iostat and htop
v04.text: Install the tools and take a short measurement. Debian/Ubuntu: `sudo apt install sysstat htop`. Rocky/Alma: htop needs EPEL, so first `sudo dnf install epel-release`.

blocks.cmd:
# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install -y sysstat htop
# Rocky / Alma
sudo dnf install -y epel-release
sudo dnf install -y sysstat htop

blocks.expected:
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st

differs: Run only the block for your distribution; the other one fails.
If `iostat` is not found, sysstat is not installed.

v05.title: Create load and find the culprit
v05.text: Warning: this task loads your CPU. Take a VM snapshot first and do this only on your own VM. The `timeout` stops the load after 30 seconds. Start it, watch it in top, find it with ps, and clean up. Press "Done" when `pgrep yes` prints nothing at the end.

blocks.cmd:
timeout 30 yes > /dev/null &
sleep 5
uptime
top -b -n 1 | head -n 12
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -n 5
pkill yes
sleep 1
pgrep yes
blocks.expected:
... the `yes` process shows about 100 %CPU at the top ...
(no output from the last command)

differs: With several cores one `yes` uses only about 100% of one core, so the load rises slowly.
If `pgrep yes` still prints a PID, run `pkill yes` again.
